title: The Rycksta stone (Sö 163), Södermanland, 1010–1050 CE — a Swedish memorial for two sons in which one of them traveled í Grikkjum, among the Greeks, and divided up gold
language_note:
Old Norse, `non`, carried in THREE registers that are all the source's own and are printed in this order on the record: the `Runtext`, a transliteration of the younger-futhark carving with its `:` word dividers; `Fornvästnordiska`, the standardised Old West Norse normalisation this corpus's readers will recognise from edited sagas; and `Runsvenska`, the Runic Swedish normalisation, which is closer to what the carver spoke. THE THIRD REGISTER IS NOT REDUNDANT and is why the excerpt carries it: `Grikkjum` and `Grikkium`, `skipti` and `skifti` differ between the two normalisations, so a reader can see the editorial distance between the language of the edition and the language of the stone.

`non` IS THE CODE FOR THE FIRST NORMALISATION AND IS BEING STRETCHED OVER THE OTHER TWO. There is no ISO 639-3 code for Runic Swedish, and the transliteration is a romanisation of runes rather than a language at all. Declared here rather than hidden: the corpus's first `non` record is also the first whose language field is a compromise.
date: 1010–1050 CE, as Runor dates it, `Vikingatid`. THE UPPER END OF THIS PROJECT'S WINDOW IS 1204, THE FOURTH CRUSADE'S SACK OF CONSTANTINOPLE, and that is what makes this record in-scope rather than late: the empire this stone's `Grikkir` names is the one whose fall the window is drawn at.
original_text_excerpt:
þruʀikr : stain : at : suni : sina : sniala : trakia : for : ulaifr : i : krikium : uli : sifti :

Þrýðríkr stein at sonu sína, snjalla drengi, fór Óleifr/Gulleifr í Grikkjum gulli skipti.

Þryðrikʀ stæin at syni sina, snialla drængia, for Olæifʀ/Gullæifʀ i Grikkium gulli skifti.
original_text_note:
Verbatim from the Runor record for Sö 163, https://app.raa.se/open/runor, `Inskrift` panel, read on 2026-09-06. Persistent object URI http://kulturarvsdata.se/uu/srdb/16595786-9444-476d-9479-52476a8373df.

THREE REGISTERS IN THE SOURCE'S ORDER AND WITH NO HEADINGS. The headings are kept out of the chunk deliberately and the reason is measured rather than stylistic: on scandinavia-06-tjurko-bracteate, twenty-six words of bracketed curatorial English pushed english_marker_ratio to 0.20 against a threshold of 0.18 and turned the whole source-language excerpt into an `english_rendering`, failing three checks at once. Measured here before the record was written: 0.12, classified `transliteration`, language `non`, retrieval-eligible.

THE NORMALISATIONS SUPPLY LETTERS THE CARVING DOES NOT HAVE, AND THEY DO IT WITHOUT BRACKETS. The transliteration reads `uli` and `sifti`; both normalisations read `gulli` and `skipti`/`skifti`. THE `g` AND THE `k` ARE THE EDITORS', restored silently — this is a normalisation and not a diplomatic edition, and it does not mark restoration the way persia-05-abnun's transcription marks its asterisks. Recorded so that a reader who counts letters between the registers does not read the difference as a capture error.

AND THE SAME SILENT `g` PRODUCES A GENUINE ALTERNATIVE READING, PRINTED BY THE EDITION. `ulaifr` in the transliteration becomes `Óleifr/Gulleifr` in one normalisation and `Olæifʀ/Gullæifʀ` in the other: the edition CANNOT DECIDE whether the name began with a carved `g` that is not there, and prints both, separated by a slash, in every register including the English. This record does not choose either.

THE CAPTURE IS NOT BLIND AND IT IS DECLARED. Located, read and pasted in one session, with no independent second reading. FINDING 55 applies in full.

WHAT DID NOT GO WRONG, CHECKED BEFORE THE RECORD WAS WRITTEN. The `ʀ` of `þruʀikr` and `Olæifʀ` is U+0280 LATIN LETTER SMALL CAPITAL R, not an ASCII `r` and not a capital; the `þ`, `Þ`, `ð`, `æ`, and the acute and ring accents are all precomposed NFC; the `:` dividers are ASCII colons with the spacing the page prints; and the trailing `:` that closes the transliteration is kept.
reference_translation:
Þryðríkr (raised) the stone in memory of his sons, able valiant men. Óleifr/Gulleifr travelled to Greece, divided (up) gold.

AND THE SAME RECORD PRINTS A SWEDISH TRANSLATION, WHICH IS NOT THE SAME SENTENCE:

”Trydrik (reste) stenen efter sina söner, goda unga män. For Olev till Grekland skiftade han guld.”

THE TWO PUBLISHED TRANSLATIONS ON ONE PAGE DIFFER ON WHO IS BEING REMEMBERED AND ON THE ALTERNATIVE NAME, AND THIS RECORD RESOLVES NEITHER. The English keeps the edition's undecided `Óleifr/Gulleifr`; the Swedish silently picks one, `Olev`. The English reads `travelled to Greece, divided (up) gold` as two clauses about Óleifr/Gulleifr; the Swedish reads `For Olev till Grekland skiftade han guld` — Olev travelled to Greece, HE divided gold — which is the same reading with an explicit pronoun the English leaves out. Both are the source's.

WHAT THE TRANSLATIONS DO WITH `Grikkium`, AND IT IS THE SECOND TIME THIS CORPUS HAS SEEN IT. The English renders it `Greece` and the Swedish `Grekland`. The word on the stone is the Old Norse name for the empire ruled from Constantinople, which in the eleventh century is the eastern Roman empire and is the empire whose fall in 1204 this project's window is drawn at. NEITHER TRANSLATION SAYS ROME AND THIS RECORD DOES NOT CORRECT THEM. persia-06-shahrestaniha carries the mirror image: a Middle Persian text calls Alexander `hrōmāyīg`, a Roman, and its published English renders it `the Greek`. Two records, two directions, one word doing two empires' work.
reference_translation_note:
The English is the `Engelska` field of the Samnordisk runtextdatabas record and the Swedish is its `Svenska` field, both served through Runor. See `translation_source`.

THE SWEDISH IS CARRIED IN THE SAME CHUNK AS THE ENGLISH ON PURPOSE. The corpus's reference_translation is English by convention, and a second published translation of the same text, on the same page, under the same edition, is evidence about the first one: it is the only thing in this record that can show a reader that the English made choices. seasia-05's rejection of an unattributed Wikipedia translation and FINDING 55's rule against a translation this project supplies itself both point the same way — the check on a translation has to come from outside this project, and here it does, from the source itself.

WHAT KIND OF TRANSLATION THIS IS. Rundata's own published English, 2020 edition, edited at the Department of Scandinavian Languages, Uppsala University, served through Riksantikvarieämbetet's Runor. Not attributed to an individual translator anywhere on the page; the corporate author is the attribution, under a named edition, at a named institution, with a persistent URI issued by a national heritage agency. Same reasoning as scandinavia-06-tjurko-bracteate, and the same reason it is not the Kedukan Bukit case.

THE BOUNDARY OF THE TRANSLATION SEARCH. What was looked at: Runor's `Engelska` and `Svenska` fields and Riksantikvarieämbetet's citation guidance. Runor names two older sigla for this stone, `L 883` and `B 821` — Liljegren's Run-urkunder and Bautil — and the scholarly convention its own guidance states is to cite the CORPUS WORK, which for a Sö signum is `Södermanlands runinskrifter` (Brate and Wessén, Sveriges runinskrifter vol. 3, Stockholm 1924–36). NONE OF THOSE THREE WAS OPENED and no claim is made about what English any of them carries. THE SEARCH STOPPED AT THE DATABASE THAT CARRIES THE TEXT.

notes:
F6, and the second of Scandinavia's two re-pointed slots (ruling 73). WITH THIS RECORD SCANDINAVIA REACHES 4 SOURCE-LANGUAGE RECORDS AGAINST A FLOOR OF 4. Two of the three regions FINDING 71 and the F6 opening state block listed below the floor are now met, and the third — Sub-Saharan Africa — is F6's remaining slot.

WHY THIS STONE, AND WHY IT SITS BESIDE THE TJURKÖ BRACTEATE RATHER THAN INSTEAD OF IT. The two records F6 places for Scandinavia are five hundred years and one direction apart, and together they are the whole shape of this region's Roman connection.

  scandinavia-06-tjurko-bracteate, 400–650: gold arrives, and a Proto-Norse
  speaker calls it `walhakurn`, THE GRAIN OF THE ROMANS, on an object that is
  an imitation of a Roman imperial medallion. The Romans are far away and the
  gold is here.

  scandinavia-07-rycksta-grikkium, 1010–1050: A MAN GOES THERE. `fór Óleifr/
  Gulleifr í Grikkjum gulli skipti` — he travelled among the Greeks and divided
  up gold. The gold is there and the Scandinavian is the one who moves.

AND THE GOLD IS IN BOTH SENTENCES. `walhakurne` and `gulli` are the same substance five centuries apart, once named after the people it came from and once shared out in their capital. Nothing in this corpus was chosen to make that pair; it is what the two inscriptions say.

WHAT THIS RECORD DOES NOT CLAIM. It does not say `Grikkir` means Byzantines, or Romans, or the Varangian Guard. The published translations say `Greece` and `Grekland` and this record quotes them and stops. The reason it is nonetheless IN SCOPE is the project's own scope statement rather than any source this session opened: the window runs to 1204, the Fourth Crusade's sack of Constantinople, so the empire ruled from that city is inside the period this corpus is about by definition, and an eleventh-century Swedish stone about a man who went there is a connection between Scandinavia and it. IF THAT IDENTIFICATION IS WRONG THE RECORD IS STILL TRUE; only its relevance would change.

NOT DECLARED GLOSS-CAPABLE, AND THIS IS THE SECOND F6 RECORD TO LEAVE THE MATERIAL ON THE TABLE. The edition prints `Óleifr/Gulleifr` — two readings of one name, separated by a slash, in every register including both translations, because it cannot decide whether an uncarved `g` belongs there. That is a genuine alternative reading inside `original_text_excerpt` and `reference_translation`, both of which the loader chunks. Ruling 77 spends F6's single gloss_capable declaration on CIH 541 and a second here would be over-delivery, which check_delivery fails on the day it happens. IF F6 CLOSES WITHOUT CIH 541, THIS RECORD AND persia-06-shahrestaniha ARE BOTH ALREADY IN THE CORPUS CARRYING GLOSS MATERIAL IN CHUNKS, and F7's declaration can be made against either without any new curation. Written down so that the option is not rediscovered.

PLACEMENT ENDS IN A REFUSAL, FOR THE SECOND TIME TODAY, AND THE SOURCE HANDED OVER TWO COORDINATES THIS TIME. Runor prints `Äldsta belagda` and `Nuvarande` WGS84 pairs — the original site and the park the stone stands in now. W1's rule forbids authoring a coordinate; Södermanland is outside the cached Pleiades coverage and the repository's only GeoNames dump is China. NEITHER COORDINATE IS COPIED INTO ANY FIELD OF THIS RECORD. A Swedish GeoNames dump would close this and scandinavia-06's placement together, and is the cheapest unclaimed piece of work F6 leaves behind.

THE PREDICTION THIS RECORD COMPLETES. Ruling 78's P3 predicted that F6's two Scandinavian records would push `vimose-runes` further down from its 7 → 16. Both are now in the index and the ranking run is what reads it.

subject_places.name: Grikkium / Grikkjum — 'Greece', among the Greeks
subject_places.note:
Where Óleifr/Gulleifr went and where he divided gold. `mentioned`, AND THE ROLE WAS CORRECTED BY THE SCHEMA RATHER THAN BY THE CURATOR. It was first written `destination`, which is what the sentence describes — a movement with a named end — and ingest.verify refused it: a directional role is relative, and with no place carrying `focus` it names one end of an edge and no other. THE REFUSAL IS RIGHT AND THE MISSING FOCUS IS A FACT ABOUT THE TEXT. The place he traveled FROM is not named on the stone; a memorial says where a man went, not where he set out from, because everyone reading it was standing there. persia-05-abnun hit the mirror image — both ends of a movement in the text and the focus a third place — and eastasia-07-tang-huiyao hit a third variant, one end missing. THREE RECORDS, THREE WAYS OF FAILING TO BE AN EDGE, and the vocabulary has one answer for all of them.

NO ID IS TAKEN. The text names a PEOPLE in the dative plural, `among the Greeks`, and the published English and Swedish render it as a country, `Greece` and `Grekland`; converting either into a city would be this record supplying a geography three sources decline to. Pleiades 423025 `Roma` is emphatically not it, and Constantinople is not named on the stone. The corpus's precedent is consistent and now three records deep: `Hrōmāy` on persia-05-abnun, `kēsar` on persia-06-shahrestaniha, and this.

subject_places.name: gulli — the gold that was divided
subject_places.note: NOT A PLACE, and it is recorded in this block because the corpus has nowhere else to record that the same substance connects this record to scandinavia-06-tjurko-bracteate, where it is called `walhakurn`, the Romans' grain. Flagged as a schema limit rather than smuggled in as geography: `subject_places` is the only structured field on a record that can point at something outside it, and what it wanted to point at here is another record. A `subject_things` block, or a record-to-record link, is the thing this corpus does not have.
